{"id": "e72146b233a241248538ceb2a522790a", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The latency spike and the queue-depth alarm on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_6 as /dev/sdf) were caused on purpose. AWS FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_5, role example-fis, tag Project=example) is running against this one volume. It started at 19:32:35Z and its injection action began at 19:32:46Z. The action is aws:ebs:volume-io-latency, set to add 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads for 60 minutes (PT60M), with no stop condition. The added delay makes each I/O take much longer, so requests pile up in the queue (VolumeQueueLength rises) even though the application sends the same amount of work. The volume is not short of capacity: before the experiment it handled about 500 write IOPS (30,000 writes per minute) at about 0.95 ms per write, which is roughly 17% of its 3,000 provisioned IOPS. Throughput is also well under the 125 MiB/s limit. Adding IOPS or throughput would not help, because the delay is added on every I/O regardless of how much capacity is provisioned. To get normal latency back, stop the experiment, or wait for it to end on its own at about 20:32:46Z. The same template has run several times today (16:15, 16:47, 18:45, all stopped by a user), which explains the earlier queue-length alarm cycles too.
## Evidence
- FIS get_experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7: status running, created 2026-11-23 19:32:34Z, action 'latency' aws:ebs:volume-io-latency started 19:32:46Z, writeIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, writeIOPercentage=100, readIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, readIOPercentage=50, duration PT60M, stopConditions none, target resourceArns=[volume/vol-0123456789abcdef0]
- FIS list_experiments: earlier runs of the same template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 on 2026-11-23 at 07:40, 08:35, 16:15, 16:47 and 18:45 (all stopped by a user or completed)
- EC2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, 20 GiB, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_6 as /dev/sdf, tagged Name=example-d-gp3-fis
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS 19:03–19:32Z (before injection): VolumeWriteOps about 30,000 per minute (~500 IOPS); VolumeTotalWriteTime about 28.6 s per minute, so about 0.95 ms per write; VolumeQueueLength about 0.77. The volume was well under its provisioned limits.
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS 19:00–19:02Z: the busiest stretch, at ~1,500 IOPS and ~0.95 ms per write, still only half of the 3,000 IOPS limit. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints showing a limit was exceeded.
- CloudWatch alarm example-d-gp3-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength \u003e 4): last changed state at 18:59:48Z (back to OK after the previous FIS run). It is expected to fire again now that injection started at 19:32:46Z.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_6
- [redacted ARN]
- example-d-gp3-queue-length
## Gaps
- CloudWatch EBS metrics for the minutes after injection began (19:33Z onward) had not been published when checked, so the rise in latency and queue length after 19:32:46Z is inferred from the experiment settings, not seen in the metrics.
- I did not check who started the experiment (the CloudTrail StartExperiment caller).
- Application-level latency metrics and logs on i-1234567890abcdef0_6 were not examined.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

- **The experiment:** `EXP1234567890abcdef_7` (template `EXT1234567890abcdef_5`, "example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency") is running against `vol-0123456789abcdef0` only.
  - CloudTrail shows the `Admin/example-session` session started it at 19:32:35Z from the AWS CLI. The template had been updated three seconds earlier.
  - Its `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` action began at 19:32:46Z. It delays 100% of writes and 50% of reads by 500 ms for 60 minutes.
  - It has no stop conditions, so it will run until about 20:32:46Z unless someone stops it.
- **The effect has already started:**
  - Before injection (19:03–19:32Z), writes averaged 0.95 ms and VolumeQueueLength was 0.77.
  - In the 19:33Z minute, average write latency was already 22.9 ms and the queue 8.58, even though that minute only partly overlapped the injection.
  - The alarm `example-d-gp3-queue-length` (queue > 4 for 3 minutes) still showed OK when I checked. It should flip to ALARM within minutes.
  - EBS metrics after 19:33Z had not been published yet, so the next part is based on the earlier run.
- **What the next hour should look like:** the 18:45 run of the same template is a close match.
  - From 18:47 to 18:56Z, the volume handled only about 42 IOPS, roughly 1.4% of its 3,000.
  - Writes took about 508 ms and the queue held steady around 16. The application appears to keep a fixed number of I/Os in flight, so the queue fills with delayed requests.
  - That run set off the alarm from 18:49:48 to 18:59:48Z. A 16:47 run (also stopped by a user) lines up with the 16:51–16:59Z alarm.

**Why more IOPS won't help**
- **Plenty of headroom:** the volume (gp3, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s) normally runs at about 1,000 IOPS (500 reads and 500 writes per second), or 33% of its limit. Throughput is about 8 MB/s of writes. During injection, usage falls to about 1.4% of the IOPS limit.

- **One correction:** the volume did touch its 3,000 IOPS ceiling once, from 18:58 to 19:02Z. That was the queued work catching up after the previous run stopped at 18:56:49Z, not the cause of the latency.

**Root cause:** latency deliberately injected by the FIS experiment above.

- If the test should end automatically when things degrade, add an alarm-based stop condition to the template.

## Results
I recommend stopping the FIS experiment that is adding 500 ms to this volume's I/O. Adding IOPS would not fix the latency, so the answer to your question is no. I haven't run anything; the commands below are for you to run.

**Why more IOPS won't help:** experiment `EXP1234567890abcdef_7` (template `EXT1234567890abcdef_5`) is still running. It adds 500 ms to every write and half the reads on `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1). No volume or instance limit is being hit: before the injection the volume used about 1,000 of its 3,000 IOPS, and the I/O and byte balances are at 99%. More IOPS or throughput would only cost more while the latency stays.

**What I checked (19:34:52Z):**
- **Experiment:** running. It started at 19:32:46Z, runs for 60 minutes, has no stop conditions and targets only this volume.
- **Volume:** gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, attached as `/dev/sdf` to `i-1234567890abcdef0_6`.
- **Alarm:** `example-d-gp3-queue-length` still shows OK (last change 18:59:48Z). It needs 3 one-minute periods above 4, so it will probably go into ALARM soon.

**Before you stop it:** this looks like a planned chaos test in the `example` project, started by the Admin/example-session session. Stopping it ends that test early. If the owner wants it to finish and the slower writes are acceptable, the experiment ends on its own at about 20:32:46Z.

**About the plan check:** the safety review flagged one critical issue, a rule that blocks "delete/terminate" operations. I'm treating that as a false positive. Stopping the experiment deletes nothing; it only ends the injected latency and puts the volume back to how it was before, and it is the fix itself. I added a step to save the current configuration, which cleared the other issue the review raised.

---

### 1. Prepare: save the current configuration
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_5 --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXT1234567890abcdef_5-before.json
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 > fis-experiment-EXP1234567890abcdef_7-before.json
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
This saves the template as it is now (stop conditions `[{source: none}]`, role `example-fis`) so you can restore it. It also records the volume settings (3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s), which this plan does not change.

### 2. Pre-validate: confirm it is still running and get approval
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query '{status:experiment.state.status,targets:experiment.targets.Volumes.resourceArns}'
```
- Expect `status = running` with the only target `[redacted ARN]`.
- If it shows `completed` or `stopped`, skip step 3a.
- Get the experiment owner's OK to end the test early.

### 3. Apply
**a) Stop the experiment (this is the fix):**
```
aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1
```
- It deletes no data or resources; FIS just stops adding latency.
- Requests already queued under 500 ms will take a few minutes to clear. Last time, after the 18:56:49Z stop, the backlog cleared from 18:58 to 19:02Z at the full 3,000 IOPS.

**b) Optional, with the owner's agreement: add a stop condition to the template:**
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_5 --region us-east-1 \
  --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]
```
- Future runs will stop by themselves when the queue-length alarm fires.
- **Trade-off:** this alarm fires after 3 minutes with the queue above 4, which a 500 ms latency test reaches almost at once. Runs would then last only about 3–4 minutes. If the test is meant to run for the full 60 minutes, use a separate alarm with a looser threshold, such as average write latency > 1,000 ms or queue > 32 for 5 minutes.
- A run can't start while its stop-condition alarm is already in ALARM.

### 4. Post-validate

```

Add a stop condition to every FIS template that targets volumes the application uses, so a forgotten or unapproved run can't slow it down for a full hour.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Elevated VolumeQueueLength on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** Alarm example-d-gp3-queue-length (threshold > 4, Average, 60s, 3/3) breached. Its last datapoints were 16.0, 9.7 and 2.6 (18:56–18:58 UTC), and it went from ALARM to OK at 18:59:48 UTC. Volume: gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, us-east-1a, account 012345678901_1.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:56:00Z - 2026-11-23T18:59:48Z

## Findings

### Cause: 500 ms injected per-I/O latency fills the queue on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 injects 500 ms latency into vol-0123456789abcdef0 (100% of writes, 50% of reads, 60 min, no stop condition). The 18:45 run's action window (18:45:28–18:56:49) matches the queue-length and write-latency spike to the minute. The earlier alarm cycle at 16:51 lines up with the 16:47 run. The current run EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (started 19:32:35 by Admin/example-session) lines up with the new rise at 19:33 (latency 22.9 ms, IOPS halved). No capacity limits were exceeded, and the sibling volume is unaffected.
**Cascades to:** symptom-ebs-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **FIS experiments from template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 on 2026-11-23:** EXP1234567890abcdef_7 has been running since 19:32:34 UTC; user example-session updated the template at 19:32:32. Earlier runs from the same template: EXP1234567890abcdef_6 (18:45:16, stopped by user), EXP1234567890abcdef_9 (16:47), EXP1234567890abcdef_4 (16:15), EXP1234567890abcdef_10 (08:35) and EXP1234567890abcdef_5 (07:40, completed). The 18:45 run lines up with the queue-length breach that ended at about 18:59.

#### Gaps
- **Application-level latency not checked:** No application metrics or logs on i-1234567890abcdef0_6 were reviewed. Application impact is inferred from the volume's own write latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime/VolumeWriteOps).

### Root Cause: Deliberate AWS FIS latency injection (EXP1234567890abcdef_7) on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 from template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 ('example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency', role example-fis) was started at 19:32:35Z by Admin/example-session via the AWS CLI. Its aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action began at 19:32:46Z and delays 100% of writes and 50% of reads by 500 ms for PT60M. It has no stop conditions, so it runs until ~20:32:46Z. Earlier runs of the same template (16:47, 18:45) caused the earlier alarm cycles. The volume has headroom (gp3 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s, normally ~1,000 IOPS, ~33% of the limit), so adding IOPS or throughput would not help.
**Cascades to:** hyp-fis-ebs-latency

#### Supporting Observations
- **FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 targets this volume with 500 ms I/O latency:** Template 'example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency' (role example-fis) targets only [redacted ARN] with action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency: 500 ms on 100% of writes and 50% of reads, duration PT60M, no stop conditions. Experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 is running; the experiment started at 19:32:35Z and its action at 19:32:46Z. The template was last updated at 19:32:32Z.
- **18:45 FIS run's injection window matches the 18:46–18:56 spike exactly:** Experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_6 ran its latency action from 18:45:28Z until a user stopped it at 18:56:49Z. Queue length rose at 18:46 and started falling at 18:57. CloudTrail shows the current run EXP1234567890abcdef_7 was started at 19:32:35Z by the Admin role (session example-session) via aws-cli fis start-experiment. CloudTrail shows no other API activity against vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 17:30 to 19:36.
- **Queue-length alarm cycles line up with FIS runs:** The alarm example-d-gp3-queue-length went OK→ALARM at 16:51:48 and ALARM→OK at 16:59:48, during the 16:47 FIS run. It went OK→ALARM at 18:49:48 and ALARM→OK at 18:59:48, during the 18:45 run. It is still OK as of the latest check, because the new run's queue-length increase (8.58 at 19:33) has not yet lasted 3 datapoints.
- **No IOPS or throughput throttling on the instance or volume:** From 18:30 to 19:35, InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck on i-1234567890abcdef0_6 were 0 the whole time. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%, and CPU was around 0.5–1.8%. Baseline load is ~1,000 total IOPS (~500 read + ~500 write) and ~8 MiB/s of writes, well under the volume's 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s limits. At 19:33, total IOPS fell to ~500, which is the latency limiting work, not a capacity limit. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Stop FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 to end the injected 500 ms I/O latency on vol-0123456789abcdef0 (no IOPS change needed)

## Reasoning
The latency is injected by the running FIS experiment, not caused by capacity: the volume normally uses ~1,000 of 3,000 IOPS and I/O/byte balances are at 99%. Stopping the experiment removes the delay; it deletes no data or resources. This looks like a planned example chaos test (started by Admin/example-session), so get the owner's OK first; otherwise it ends on its own at ~20:32:46Z. The safety review's delete/terminate flag is treated as a false positive.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Snapshot the template, experiment and volume settings so they can be…
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_5 --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXT1234567890abcdef_5-before.json
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 > fis-experiment-EXP1234567890abcdef_7-before.json
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Snapshot the template, experiment and volume settings so they can be restored

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Verify the experiment is running and targets only this volume
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query '{status:experiment.state.status,targets:experiment.targets.Volumes.resourceArns}'
```
**Purpose:** Verify the experiment is running and targets only this volume
**Advisory:** If status is completed or stopped, skip the stop step.

#### 2.2 Avoid cutting short a planned chaos test without consent
**Type:** text
Get the experiment owner's approval to end the example test early.
**Purpose:** Avoid cutting short a planned chaos test without consent

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 End the injected latency on the volume
**Type:** command
```
aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** End the injected latency on the volume
**Risks:** Ends the planned chaos test early, Queued I/O takes a few minutes to drain at up to 3,000 IOPS

#### 3.2 Optionally make future runs stop automatically when the queue alarm…
**Type:** command
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_5 --region us-east-1 \
  --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]
```
**Purpose:** Optionally make future runs stop automatically when the queue alarm fires
**Risks:** This alarm trips after ~3 minutes, so runs would last only ~3-4 minutes
**Advisory:** For full 60-minute tests use a looser alarm (e.g. write latency > 1,000 ms or queue > 32 for 5 min)., A run cannot start while its stop-condition alarm is in ALARM.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Require a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition on FIS templates that target application volumes
**Description:** Wherever EXT1234567890abcdef_5 is defined (IaC or scripts), replace stop condition `source: none` with `aws:cloudwatch:alarm` pointing to a dedicated latency or queue alarm with the threshold the test is meant to allow, so a forgotten or unapproved run cannot degrade the application for a full hour.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The template shows a CloudWatch alarm stop condition
- A test run stops on its own within a few minutes of that alarm firing
- Template edits cannot remove the condition without review (today an edit at 19:32:32Z went straight into a run at 19:32:35Z)
